about.title: Huntington Beach Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A wet tile floor in a Beach Boulevard grocery store. An unmarked step at a Pacific Coast Highway restaurant. A cracked walkway outside an apartment complex a few blocks from the sand. Falls like these happen every week across Huntington Beach, a city of roughly 201,899 people in Orange County, and the people who get hurt are often left wondering who, if anyone, is responsible. Under California premises liability law, the answer turns on notice. You generally have to show the property owner knew about the hazard, or reasonably should have known, and then failed to repair it or warn you. That is why the first few hours matter so much: photograph the exact spot, note the time, collect names of anyone who saw what happened, and ask that surveillance footage be preserved before it is overwritten. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects injured Huntington Beach residents and visitors with an independent personal injury attorney who takes premises cases on contingency, meaning no fee unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Huntington Beach Fall Victims Turn to LawProactive

items.title: Attorneys Who Understand the Notice Requirement
items.desc: California asks fall victims to show the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. The attorneys in our network build that proof from inspection logs, prior complaints, and how long the condition existed.

items.title: Fast Action on Surveillance Video
items.desc: Stores, restaurants, and apartment buildings along Beach Boulevard and Pacific Coast Highway frequently record their premises, but footage can be erased within days. An early preservation demand keeps that evidence available.

items.title: Clear Guidance on Deadlines and Shared Fault
items.desc: Most California premises claims carry a two-year filing window, but it is much shorter when a city, county, or state agency owns the property. Even if you were partly at fault, pure comparative fault means you may still recover a reduced share.

items.question: I fell on the Huntington Beach Pier walkway. Is that treated differently than a fall in a store?
items.answer: Yes, and the difference matters a great deal. When a public entity such as the City of Huntington Beach, Orange County, or the State of California owns or maintains the property, you must generally file a formal government claim within a much shorter period than the two-year deadline that applies to private owners. Missing that shorter window can end the claim before it starts, so an attorney should review the situation quickly.

items.question: The store manager said I wasn't paying attention. Does that mean I have no case?
items.answer: Not under California law. The state follows pure comparative fault, which means your recovery is reduced by whatever share of responsibility is assigned to you, but it is not wiped out. If the owner knew about the hazard or should have discovered it and failed to fix or warn about it, they can still be held partly responsible even if you were also distracted.

items.question: What should I do in the first day or two after a fall in Huntington Beach?
items.answer: Get medical care first, even if the pain seems manageable, because fall injuries often worsen over the following days. Then document the hazard with photos, write down the time and exact location, and gather contact information for any witnesses. Ask the property owner in writing to preserve any surveillance video, and reach out to LawProactive so an independent attorney can send a formal preservation request before the footage is lost.
